title: Adani Settles US Fraud Case for $18 Million as Criminal Charges Near Collapse
excerpt: The settlement with the SEC marks a turning point for the Adani Group—but questions linger about corporate governance and diaspora investor confidence
body:
The Adani Group's long-running legal troubles in the United States appear to be drawing to a close. Gautam Adani, the Indian infrastructure magnate, and his nephew Sagar Adani have agreed to pay $18 million to settle civil fraud allegations brought by the US Securities and Exchange Commission—a deal that, if approved by a federal court, could clear the path for criminal charges against Adani to be dropped entirely.

## The Reckoning That Wasn't

The settlement, announced this week, resolves SEC claims that the Adanis made false and misleading statements to American investors in connection with a 2021 bond offering by Adani Green Energy Ltd. Under the terms, Gautam Adani will pay $6 million and Sagar Adani $12 million in civil penalties, without admitting or denying wrongdoing. Both have agreed to permanent injunctions barring future violations of US securities anti-fraud laws.

The SEC's original complaint, filed in late 2024, was explosive. It alleged that the Adanis had participated in a scheme involving over $250 million in bribes paid to Indian government officials to secure lucrative solar energy contracts—contracts that underpinned the bond sale to US investors. The case sent shockwaves through Indian capital markets and raised uncomfortable questions about corporate governance at India's fastest-growing conglomerate.

## A Parallel Track

On the criminal side, the US Department of Justice had filed parallel charges against Adani, making him one of the highest-profile Indian businessmen ever to face a federal indictment in America. But prosecutors are now reportedly considering dropping those charges, according to people familiar with the matter. Adani's legal team, led by lawyers at Sullivan & Cromwell, had argued aggressively that the case lacked jurisdiction, that the alleged bribery occurred entirely in India, and that the SEC's reach into foreign sovereign affairs was legally flawed.

The potential collapse of the criminal case represents a significant victory for Adani, whose lawyers had also filed a formal motion to dismiss, citing extraterritorial overreach. A pre-motion conference was granted by US District Judge Nicholas Garaufis in New York, signalling judicial receptivity to the defence's arguments.

## Markets Respond

Investor confidence in the Adani Group, battered since the Hindenburg Research short-seller report in early 2023 and further shaken by the 2024 indictment, has been cautiously recovering. The settlement removes a critical overhang that had complicated the group's ability to raise capital in international markets. Analysts suggest it could unlock a planned $10 billion pipeline of US investments and allow Adani Green Energy to resume its aggressive expansion in renewable energy.

Adani Group shares rallied on Indian bourses following news of the settlement, with Adani Green Energy rising over 4% in early trading. Broader market sentiment was also lifted by the prospect of restored foreign institutional investor interest.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian investors and NRIs with exposure to Adani stocks—a constituency that has grown substantially over the past decade—the settlement offers a measure of closure, even if it leaves questions unanswered. The case had become a political football in India, with opposition leader Rahul Gandhi accusing Prime Minister Modi of negotiating a "release deal" for Adani rather than a genuine trade agreement during recent US-India talks.

The broader lesson for diaspora investors is one of due diligence. The Adani saga exposed how rapidly a single legal action in a foreign jurisdiction can crater the value of Indian-listed shares, particularly those held by global funds. For NRIs managing portfolios that span both US and Indian markets, the episode is a reminder that regulatory risk knows no borders.

## What Comes Next

The settlement requires final court approval, which is expected within weeks. If the DOJ formally drops criminal charges, the Adani Group will have navigated what many considered an existential legal threat—at a financial cost that, for a conglomerate with a market capitalisation exceeding $200 billion, amounts to a rounding error. But the reputational cost, and the precedent set by the SEC's willingness to pursue Indian corporate titans on American soil, will linger far longer.
